𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐌𝐎𝐕𝐈𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐀𝐋𝐌𝐎𝐒𝐓 𝐁𝐀𝐍𝐊𝐑𝐔𝐏𝐓𝐄𝐃 𝟐𝟎𝐭𝐡 𝐂𝐄𝐍𝐓𝐔𝐑𝐘 𝐅𝐎𝐗⁣ 👀 
⁣
𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐫𝐚 (𝟏𝟗𝟔𝟑) was supposed to be one of Hollywood’s greatest spectacles. Instead, its production became so expensive that it nearly brought 20th Century Fox to its knees. The movie was originally budgeted at only a few million dollars, but almost everything that could go wrong did. Production began in England before being abandoned after Elizabeth Taylor became seriously ill. Sets were scrapped and rebuilt in Rome, the director was replaced, the script was constantly rewritten, and filming stretched on for years. Taylor’s relationship with Richard Burton also became an international scandal, bringing even more attention to an already troubled production.⁣
⁣
By the time the movie was finished, its cost had reached around $44 million, an extraordinary amount in 1963. Using U.S. inflation, that would be roughly $470 million in 2026 money, making it one of the most expensive movies ever produced when adjusted for inflation. The enormous spending contributed to major financial problems at Fox, forcing the studio to cut costs, sell assets and halt other productions.⁣
⁣
Despite being the highest-grossing film of 1963, its huge cost meant that ticket sales alone couldn’t immediately rescue it. Television rights and later re-releases eventually helped Cleopatra break even around 1973. The movie that almost destroyed a studio ultimately survived to become exactly what Fox had wanted in the first place: a Hollywood epic people are still talking about more than sixty years later.

source_details.title: Caesar and Cleopatra
source_details.synopsis: Caesar and Cleopatra is a 1945 British historical romantic film directed by Gabriel Pascal which was a film adaptation of George Bernard Shaw's 1901 play of the same title. The film stars Vivien Leigh and Claude Rains in the title roles. Some scenes were directed by Brian Desmond Hurst, who took no formal credit. The picture was produced by Independent Producers and Pascal Film Productions and distributed by Eagle-Lion Distributors. Upon release, Caesar and Cleopatra failed to earn back its colossal budget. John Bryan was nominated for an Oscar for Best Art Direction.
